common_name: Hamari Bride Dahlia (White Large Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after soil has warmed; stake at planting time to support the heavy white blooms.

directions: Hamari Bride belongs to the celebrated British Hamari series of large decorative exhibition dahlias, the same breeding line that produced Hamari Gold and Hamari Girl, and is grown chiefly for its crisp white, fully double blooms that can open 8 inches or more across on a vigorous, upright plant. Like its siblings, it holds its clean color well through hot weather and has long been a dependable choice on the British show bench for growers wanting a pure white giant decorative. Stake plants early to support the heavy flower heads, feed regularly through the growing season, and disbud surrounding side buds if the largest possible blooms are the goal. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.

common_name: Strawberry Ice Dahlia (Giant Pink-Lavender-Cream Formal Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed; stake well before the plant reaches full size, since the giant blooms are heavy.

directions: Strawberry Ice is a giant formal decorative dahlia whose huge, many-petaled blooms blend soft pink, lavender, and creamy tones in a single flower, a color combination close enough to its better-known counterpart Kidd's Climax that the two are sometimes confused on the show bench. Flowers can open 10 inches or more across in good culture, carried on a tall, vigorous plant that needs staking well before buds appear. Disbud the side shoots around each developing flower to channel energy into fewer, larger blooms if exhibition size is the goal, and feed regularly through the growing season. Lift tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8 and store them in a cool, dry place over winter.

common_name: Yellow Augusta Chrysanthemum (Yellow Quill-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, staking stems early to support the quilled bloom.

directions: Yellow Augusta is a Dutch-bred quill-type exhibition chrysanthemum remembered today chiefly as one of the two parents, alongside Dark Flamenco, behind the popular spider-flowered cultivar Westland. Its narrow, hollow ray florets curl into tight, bright golden-yellow quills around a darker central disc, opening slowly on strong, upright stems in the classic exhibition quill form. As with other show-bench mums, it performs best grown as a single disbudded stem, with side buds removed as they appear to concentrate the plant's energy into one large terminal bloom. Propagate fresh cuttings each spring from overwintered stock rather than relying on an aging clump, and stake plants early to support the heavy flower head.

common_name: Dark Flamenco Chrysanthemum (Dark Red-Bronze Quill-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, staking stems early to support the quilled bloom.

directions: Dark Flamenco is a Dutch-bred quill-type exhibition chrysanthemum known chiefly as the other parent, alongside Yellow Augusta, of the widely grown spider-flowered cultivar Westland. Its narrow, hollow ray florets curl into tight quills of a deep, smoldering red-bronze that gave the cultivar its name, surrounding a dark central disc on sturdy, upright stems. Like other show-bench quill and spider mums, it is traditionally grown as a single disbudded stem, with side buds pinched out as they form to direct all of the plant's energy into one large terminal flower. Take fresh cuttings from overwintered stock plants each spring, and stake early to support the heavy bloom.

planting.note: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep, in October-November in zone 9; Burgundy is a Creole type that needs little winter chill to bulb reliably.

directions: Burgundy is a Creole-type softneck garlic named for the deep purple-red streaking on its clove wrappers, one of a small group of regional Creole selections — alongside Ajo Rojo, Creole Red, and Pescadero Red — bred for the mild, low-chill winters of the Gulf South and similar hot, humid climates. Like other Creole garlics it forms a tight, symmetrical bulb of roughly 8 to 12 plump cloves with a rich, moderately hot flavor and notably better storage life than most northern hardneck types. Because it needs little cold exposure to trigger bulbing, it performs reliably in zone 9 gardens where Rocambole and Porcelain garlics often fail without pre-chilling. Harvest once the lower leaves have browned and 4 to 5 green leaves remain, then cure in a shaded, airy spot for several weeks before storage.
sources: Gourmet Garlic Gardens — Creole garlic variety descriptions
